content: An observational science is a branch of science in which it is not feasible to design or conduct controlled experiments within the domain of study. For instance, in the field of astronomy, it is impossible to create or manipulate stars or galaxies to observe the outcomes of such interventions. Other examples of sciences that are inherently observational include geology, paleontology, epidemiology, and many areas within the social sciences. Certain scientific disciplines may encompass both observational and experimental components. For example, in high-energy physics, some interactions involving energy levels that exceed what can be generated in laboratory experiments can only be observed indirectly through astronomical observations. To address the limitations of not being able to directly perform controlled experiments as part of the scientific method, two primary strategies are employed. First, multivariate statistical techniques are used to approximate experimental control by applying statistical control. Second, experimental observations of previously unobserved phenomena can be utilized to propose new hypotheses and test existing ones. This approach effectively leverages pre-existing natural experiments. In the social sciences, disciplines such as sociology and economics are generally considered observational sciences due to the impracticality—and often the ethical concerns—of manipulating entire societies or economies for experimental purposes. However, microeconomics can be classified as an experimental science because it is possible to construct experimental microeconomic systems. In some cases, fields of study can transition from being purely observational to becoming experimental. For example, the study of comets was exclusively observational until the early 21st century. This changed in 2005 when the first human-engineered collision with a comet was successfully carried out, marking a shift toward experimental investigation in this area.
